name: Water-powered factory system in the Derwent Valley
summary: Richard Arkwright's water-powered cotton-spinning mills at Cromford, begun in 1771, became the blueprint for factory production and were copied across Britain and later abroad.
description: Arkwright began a water-powered spinning mill at Cromford in 1771 and a larger second mill in 1776-77, and UNESCO says the 'Arkwright System' was truly established with the second. The Derbyshire Historic Environment Record calls the system a blueprint for factory production that was soon replicated elsewhere in Britain and later in other parts of the world. UNESCO's account of the valley begins with the Lombe brothers' silk mill at Derby of 1721, whose machinery followed an Italian design and whose scale and workforce it calls without precedent.

impact.note: Factories on this pattern were replicated across Britain and then the world, so that factory work and factory-made goods came to shape most people's lives (reach 3) and the household gave way to the factory as the place of work (depth 3); mill building and industrial organisation grew from it as a line of work rather than as a platform for many fields (generativity 2).

date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The Silk Mill at Derby was built in 1721 for the brothers John and Thomas Lombe and housed silk-throwing machinery based on an Italian design; UNESCO treats it as the start of the valley's mills, before the factory system proper.

evidence.supports: Derby in 1721 for the brothers John and Thomas Lombe, which housed machinery for throwing silk, based on an Italian design

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Was Lombe's 1721 Derby mill water-powered, and did Arkwright's mills draw on it or on Italian silk mills? The sources read do not say.
The water-driven silk-throwing mills of Bologna and Piedmont, the main rival claim to the first factories, were not examined.
A UNESCO nomination document was reported in a search result to give 1727 for the Derby mill; this was not checked.
earliest_record points at 1771 because the sources place the factory system's establishment with Arkwright; if the Derby silk mill is judged a factory, the date becomes 1721.

research.note: UNESCO says the Derwent Valley 'saw the birth of the factory system', but its own account starts with the 1721 Derby silk mill, whose machinery was 'based on an Italian design', and the Italian silk mills were not examined, so priority and independence are unsettled.
